To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) A three-level atomic system can be made transparent for a resonant probe photon field by the application of a strong control laser field on an atomic transition to a highly excited Rybberg state, and (b) The long-range dipole-dipole interaction between the atoms in the Rydbeck state can be used to replace the control field and induce transparency for a resonant field of probe photons, with the number of photons limited by the number of spins.

a three-level atomic medium, in which one of the levels is a long-lived state (such as a highly excited Ryberg state), can be made transparent for a number of photons not exceeding the number np of atoms prepared in the long-lived state.

a three-level atomic system can be rendered transparent to a resonantly tuned probe field in the vicinity of a long-lived Rydberg state by a single or a small number of spin-1/2 atoms prepared in the Rybderg state, with all the probe photons resonantly absorbed upon their transmission through the medium.

the development of a new class of quantum optical devices that are based on the long-range interactions between Rydberg atoms and can be used for quantum computation, quantum communication and single photon sources.
quantum information and quantum optics with Rydberg atom systems.
quantum information processing using the long-range interactions of highly excited Rydbergs states of atoms.

the dipole–dipeole interaction between a single Rydberg atom and a single photon induces the phenomenon of induced transparency in a three-level medium of atoms.

the Rydberg atoms in the long-lived states are able to induce transparency for the probe field in a dense medium of atoms with the aid of dipole–dipe interactions.
the Rydberg atoms can act as a single photon source and also a single photon router.
a single spin atom can be used as a quantum logic gate for a single photon, and a number of spin atoms as a quantum logic gates for a number of photons.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single spin can be used to control the transparency of an optically dense atomic medium.

the Rydberg states, which are known to play a key role in many quantum optical phenomena such as Rydberg blockade and electromagnetically induced transparency, are also useful for achieving quantum logic gates and quantum memory.
